securityFindings.title: The public MCP subregistry published private-network URLs declared outside remotes[]

securityFindings.title: metadataCacheKey composes its parts with the length after the part, so the composition is not injective
securityFindings.impact: Defence in depth only. The key is `${tenantId ?? ''}#${tenantId?.length ?? 0}#${issuer}`. Because the length follows its part rather than preceding it, ('a', '3#x') and ('a#1', 'x') both produce 'a#1#3#x'. Two tenants would then share one cached authorization-server metadata document. Not reachable today: tenant identifiers match /^[a-zA-Z0-9_.:@/-]{1,200}$/ and so cannot contain '#', and assertIssuerIdentifier runs before the key is built and rejects an issuer with a fragment. No exploit exists; the composition should still be the injective one.

securityFindings.proposedPatch: In src/server/connectors/auth/discovery.ts, replace the body of metadataCacheKey with: return `${(tenantId ?? '').length}:${tenantId ?? ''}|${issuer}`; This is the length-prefixed form charter section 3.1 recommends. It changes cache keys, which only invalidates an in-process cache.
securityFindings.resolution: Fixed by the integrator. metadataCacheKey is length-prefixed: `${tenant.length}:${tenant}|${issuer.length}:${issuer}`, so every part is self-delimiting and no arrangement of the parts composes to another's string. tests/connectors/auth/cache-key.test.ts asserts the named collision and then the general property over 2000 generated pairs, because 83 auth tests passed with the broken key: nothing had asked the question.

securityFindings.title: The registry importer redacts a declared value only when the publisher set isSecret
securityFindings.impact: A publisher who pastes a credential into environmentVariables[].value and forgets isSecret gets that value stored verbatim in the normalized definition and republished by exportDefinitionProjection(definition, { includeNativeExtensions: true }). The public subregistry projection does apply a name heuristic (sensitiveName matches token, secret, api-key, password, credential, authorization, cookie, private), so the two surfaces in the same module disagree about what a secret is. No public leak today: the default export, the agent projection and the public subregistry all exclude it, and includeNativeExtensions is an operator opt-in the export docstring already warns about.
securityFindings.reproduction: importServerJson with packages[0].environmentVariables = [{ name: 'GITHUB_TOKEN', value: 'ghp_CANARY_PLAIN' }, { name: 'MARKED', value: 'ghp_CANARY_MARKED', isSecret: true }]. securityFindings.title: The event mount point is evaluated before the request boundary and before the request budget
securityFindings.impact: createConnectorHttp checks path.startsWith('/events/') before assertRequestBoundary and before reserveRequest. That is correct for an unauthenticated provider delivery authenticated by signature, and this swarm confirmed the route cannot reach any command route: '/events/nango/extra', '/events/', '/events/../connections' and '/events/%2e%2e/connections' all fall through to undefined, a GET is 405, and a malformed authority is 404. The consequence is that this layer applies no rate limit to the events path, so whatever bound exists must come from the mounted receiver.
securityFindings.reproduction: tests/connectors/security/command-boundary.test.ts 'the event mount point authenticates by signature and reaches nothing else'.
securityFindings.proposedPatch: Integrator: confirm the events receiver supplied at mount time carries its own per-authority bound, or add an authority-scoped budget to createConnectorEventsHttp. No code change proposed here because the receiver is not this swarm's module.
securityFindings.integratorConfirmation: Confirmed by the integrator, and the answer is partly no. The receiver has its own body bound: it refuses a declared content-length over the ceiling before reading, and reads the stream bounded regardless, so an oversized delivery cannot be used to exhaust memory. Dedupe prevents reprocessing. What it does not have is a request-rate ceiling of its own, so the observation stands: the events path bypasses the per-subject budget and nothing replaces it, and an unauthenticated flood costs one signature verification per delivery before anything rejects it. Not fixed here, deliberately. The only correct key is the authority the route names, since there is no subject on this path, and the ceiling has to be chosen against real delivery volume for the busiest provider a deployment subscribes to. Picking one blind, at the end of this work, on a production request path, to close an informational finding, trades a modest gain for a real risk of refusing legitimate deliveries. Recommended shape for whoever sets it: a per-authority bound in the receiver policy, applied after the route resolves and before verification, answering 429.

A skill's effect, data classification and cost are recorded as `unknown`: A2A declares none of them, and guessing from a name or a tag would be an invented claim.
Only the JSONRPC protocol binding is executable; GRPC and HTTP+JSON interfaces import with an explicit unsupported diagnostic.

Task identity is owner-bound: the caller holds `a2atask:<sha256>`, a digest correlation key; the upstream task id lives only in protected handoff material. Resolution checks tenant, subject, connection, binding and connection generation, so a leaked reference cannot cancel or continue another principal's task.

Only skills listed in the binding's approvedSkills may be delegated, and each must map to a bound operation whose transport is `delegated` with route `a2a-skill:<id>` on the agent's destination. Card claims never widen this.

start, input and cancel are journaled through the effect journal before the call; a repeated command id returns the journaled outcome instead of a second task, and a lost response on a non-read delegation is `indeterminate`, not a retryable failure.

Artifacts are described, never fetched. A URL part is reported as `retrieval: not-fetched` with the URL withheld from the caller entirely. `retrieveArtifact` is privileged-internal, off unless a host enables it, requires an explicit approval object, and refuses any origin that is not an approved destination of the binding.
Streaming (message/stream, SSE) and push-notification configuration are not implemented; progress is polled through an approved status operation. Reported unsupported with the reason.

Verification compares the served card with the reviewed one (name, profile, interface URL, protocol version) and records `credential-accepted` plus `resource-access`. It deliberately asserts no account identity: an Agent Card is the agent's own statement.
A2A publishes no connection resource and no revocation operation, so disconnect is local-only and revoke is unsupported; both report the exact native limitation.
Owner kinds `user` and `organization` are accepted; `workload` is refused rather than silently mapped to the signed-in subject.

Seven transport-neutral intents (list, inspect, status, connect, operations, reconnect, disconnect) over a narrow dependency interface; the command service supplies it and rechecks capability, ownership, generation and policy itself.

Connections leave through agentConnectorProjection and definitions through agentDefinitionProjection. Approved operations have no core projection, so they leave through a local positive allowlist (agentOperationProjection) that omits transport, method, path template, tool name, destination id and authentication profile.
Additive on the MCP server: registerAgentConnectorTools skips any name already registered, so the MCP swarm's connector_catalog/status/connect/invoke are untouched and only five names are added.

The service wiring (an AgentConnectorDependencies built over ConnectorCommandService) is the integrator's mount; these tests exercise the intents against an in-memory dependency and a fake MCP server, so the evidence level is unit rather than local-integration.

Feature detection reuses the existing browserModelContext() unchanged, so the connector tools and the ceremony tools cannot drift apart; the mount also reports which spelling was found (document or navigator).
No native model context means no registration and no installation of anything: the absent API stays absent, there is no polyfill, and the application's ordinary controls are the whole experience.

Ownership is by AbortSignal, as the draft specifies. A mount records exactly the names it registered, refuses a second mount of a live name, and unmounts by aborting only its own controller; tools another owner registered are untouched.
`exposedTo` is never passed, so nothing here claims to drive an iframe or another origin; the mount reports crossOriginExposure: "not-requested".
Annotations are hints. The dispatcher is never told about them and the server never sees them; a rewritten readOnlyHint changes nothing.

Supported-native-browser evidence here is a spec-shaped model-context double in Node, NOT a real browser. Real-browser (Playwright) evidence is not claimed; browser suites cannot be run while other swarms hold the fixed ports.

One decision function for HTTP, MCP, WebMCP and A2A. Every test asks the same question on all four surfaces and asserts one answer, so a surface with its own opinion fails rather than becoming the deployment's real policy.

A WebMCP call is delegated work by construction: it runs inside the person's own browser session, so the session alone cannot distinguish it from that person clicking a button, and the surface is used instead.

A stop halts connect, operate, delegate and administer; read and disconnect stay possible so a stop does not strand the person. It is evaluated before any lookup, so it cannot be used to probe for a connection's existence.

Covered denials: assistant-stopped, role-revoked, connection-not-owned, connection-missing, connection-inactive, generation-fenced, binding-revised, policy-revised, configuration-revised. Each maps to one connector error code on every transport.

DelegationStopRegistry is an in-process default with length-prefixed composite keys; a deployment backs the same `readStop` shape with the shared encrypted store. That durable implementation is the state swarm's / integrator's.
The A2A leg of AC-AG-04 is exercised against the real adapter and the loopback agent double; the HTTP and MCP legs are exercised through the guard, not through a mounted route table.
An app definition carries no identifier or display name; the host supplies both and an info diagnostic says so.

`custom`, `session`, `digest` and `oauth1` authentication map to an unsupported native profile with a blocking security diagnostic: Zapier states where a credential goes only inside middleware code, and this reader will not guess it. The auth fields still import as configuration.

`oauth2` maps to oauth-authorization-code only when `authorizeUrl` and `getAccessToken` are literal https URLs without `{{curlies}}`; otherwise the profile is unsupported native `zapier-oauth2-dynamic`.
Resource-generated actions are identified as `<resourceKey>.<method>` because the platform's generated key is not stated in the definition; an info diagnostic records that.
Dynamic dropdowns (`dynamic`, `search`, `choices.perform`) and function-valued field lists produce diagnostics and definition-level limitations; their options are never fetched.
`beforeRequest`/`afterResponse`/`hydrators` are recorded inert and never applied to any host request.
A programmatic node (an `execute`, `webhook`, `poll` or `trigger` method) reports `invoke: unsupported` and the limitation "programmatic node requires host runtime"; its metadata still imports.
An expression (any value beginning with `=`) is preserved verbatim as inert text and never evaluated; a routing URL or base URL that is an expression yields no approved destination.
An n8n node does not declare whether an operation reads or writes, so every imported operation records `effect: unknown` with an info diagnostic. An HTTP method is not a declaration.

A credential maps to an executable profile only from a literal `authenticate.properties` placement (`header`, `qs`, `auth`); a body placement and an inherited `oAuth2Api` credential are unsupported with a blocking security diagnostic.
`methods.loadOptions` is never invoked; option lists it would produce are not part of the description.
The node icon, the compiled package and the node's own code are outside the description; the export says the node cannot run from it.

Workato publishes no non-Ruby serialization, so `workato-static-profile/1` is this repository's own format, documented in src/server/connectors/formats/workato/profile.ts. A Ruby lambda is spelled `{"$lambda": true}` in it.

From Ruby source only literal hash entries are read: connection fields, the authorization type, action and trigger names, and field lists written as literal arrays. Every lambda, block, heredoc, interpolated string, backtick command and method call is an inert diagnostic.

`api_key` maps to an executable profile only when the static profile declares `authorization.apply` as `{placement, parameter}`; from Ruby the placement lives in a lambda and the profile is unsupported native `workato-api-key-placement`.
`oauth2` needs literal `authorization_url` and `token_url`; the SDK writes them as lambdas, so the Ruby path reports `workato-oauth2-dynamic`.
The client-credentials grant, which the SDK writes as `custom_auth` with an `acquire` lambda, maps only from an explicit `authorization.oauth2 = {grant: "client_credentials", token_url}` declaration.
A Workato action does not declare whether it reads or writes, so actions record `effect: unknown`; triggers record `read`.
A connector carries no version of its own; the host supplies one and an info diagnostic says so.
`base_uri` is a lambda in idiomatic Ruby, so the Ruby path derives no approved destination from it.

The wire contract is Ceremony's own; no vendor publishes one. A deployment must register an endpoint that implements it. `verifyExternalRuntimeSignature` is exported so a host implements verification with the same code the adapter signs with.

The input and output shape language is deliberately not JSON Schema: no $ref, no composition, no `pattern`, no `format`. A caller-supplied regular expression is an execution primitive and is refused at binding-parse time.
Evidence is protocol-fixture against a loopback runtime. No vendor runtime was contacted and no live authorization exists.
A repeated request digest returns the journalled prior outcome for anything but a genuinely read-only operation; it never re-issues the call.

The round trip is defined over the supported subset (`automationSupportedSubset`): identity, display, authentication profiles, configuration, events, declared servers and each capability's descriptive fields plus the native extension keys the exporter documents. Diagnostics and digests are deliberately outside it, because an export legitimately produces its own diagnostics.

No export is runnable on its target platform. Zapier's export replaces a function with the platform's own `$func$0$f$` marker; n8n's carries the node description without its package or code; Workato's carries `{"$lambda": true}` markers. Each reports the loss.
A security-critical loss (a credential placement that was never imported) is reported as blocking with `blocks-authorization`.
Pinned to the released catalog tag v4.22.0 of apache/camel-kamelets (retrieved 2026-09-18); a newer catalog is a new pin, never an automatic upgrade.
The Camel route template, dataTypes block and Maven dependency list are preserved as inert data: nothing is evaluated, resolved or deployed.
A source Kamelet's delivery transport is a Camel component, not an HTTP webhook, so the event descriptor is transport unsupported with the native scheme preserved.
No live catalog fetch was performed from a test; fixtures are locally authored documents shaped exactly like the released ones.

Binding directions are taken from the supported-bindings component reference (docs.dapr.io, runtime v1.18, retrieved 2026-09-18) for the sixteen types that page states; any other component type is reported direction unknown and unverified rather than guessed.

There is no discover dimension: Dapr documents no sidecar component-inventory endpoint, and asking one for its loaded components would be the unauthenticated inventory surface this adapter exists to refuse.
There is no verify dimension: a sidecar exposes no account or identity endpoint, so connectivity could only be relabelled as identity.
Dapr defines no idempotency key for a binding invocation, so an interrupted write is journalled indeterminate and never retried automatically.

A Dapr input delivery carries no provider event id; deduplication therefore uses host-assigned identity, and the app API token carries no timestamp so this leg cannot be replay-bounded by the signature itself.
Disconnect is local only: Dapr offers a platform caller no operation to delete a component, unload it from a sidecar or revoke a sidecar token.

Provision, deprovision, update, bind and unbind are not implemented: the module contains no request builder for them and every bound operation must be a GET with effect read, so the default profile cannot issue a state-changing request even if a binding asked it to.

Fetching an instance or a binding is attempted only when the reviewed catalog declared instances_retrievable or bindings_retrievable. The specification defines no error for calling an unsupported fetch endpoint, so an absent flag is reported as a native limitation and the endpoint is never probed.
Paid plans are recorded as out of scope: no plan change and no provisioning of a non-free plan is available here.
A fetched instance is the broker's assertion about its own record; the verification claim says so and asserts nothing about the underlying resource, and no permissions are inferred.
Binding rotation, volume mounts, syslog drains and route services are described but not exercised; only their presence is reported.
Basic authentication is the specification's default platform-to-broker mechanism and the only one implemented; out-of-band mechanisms are explicitly out of scope in the specification itself.

The default KameletHostRunnerPort is unavailable and fail-closed; its reason names that no Camel runner is configured and that Ceremony starts no JVM, resolves no dependency and deploys no integration.
A deployment whose runtime class is browser cannot be given a runner at all: construction throws, so no code path exists in which a browser-only deployment reports local execution.
A configured remote runner is unavailable until its signing-secret configuration is present; an unsigned delegation is never sent.

The delegation signature is a host-internal scheme (HMAC-SHA256 over v1:timestamp:nonce:descriptor-digest), not a vendor protocol; it is not a claim of interoperability with any Camel distribution's own API.
All evidence is protocol-fixture. No vendor account, broker, sidecar or Camel runtime was contacted, and nothing here is live or vendor-certified.

The three doubles are written from the published documentation and decide conformance themselves; none of them calls the implementation under test, including the Camel runner double, which recomputes the delegation HMAC with node:crypto rather than using the signing helper.
Smithery's catalog exposes no server version; identities carry nativeVersion "unversioned" and a smithery.version.not-exposed diagnostic rather than an invented version.
Pagination is Smithery's page/pageSize with a pagination envelope; the adapter reports page numbers as cursors and never follows an upstream-supplied URL.
A stdio bundle connection is preserved as an unsupported profile with a blocking issue: no bundle is downloaded or executed.
Live evidence blocked: no authorized Smithery account or API key in this environment.
Smithery reports connection state only; it exposes no upstream account identity, so claims carry that limitation and no exact-account verification is asserted.
Upstream revocation is unsupported: deleting a managed connection ends the brokered session and does not revoke the provider grant.
Runtime calls need a host-supplied McpClientPort; without one the invoke capability row is unsupported.
Live evidence blocked: no authorized Smithery namespace or service token in this environment.
Local execution is unavailable by default: unavailableHostRunner reports the exact reason and the invoke capability row is unsupported with runtime trusted-local-runner.
Docker publishes no JSON schema for the catalog file; the field set was taken from the documentation and from the served catalog, and unknown fields are noted by name rather than carried.
Entries whose authorization is performed by the Docker MCP Toolkit are preserved with a blocking authorize diagnostic; Ceremony does not run the Toolkit.
Export is only possible for definitions that originated from a Docker catalog; values redacted on import are never reconstructed.
PulseMCP documents /v0beta as deprecated with a sunset by September 2026; the capability row carries that sentence.
The native listing exposes no version, tools or configuration schema, so definitions record that rather than inventing them.

Sub-registry entries wrap a server.json document; importing one requires the MCP registry importer to be wired in, otherwise the import capability row is unsupported and the entry stays discoverable only.
Live evidence blocked: no PulseMCP tenant API key in this environment.
Suggestions only: the module merges nothing and exposes no way to accept a suggestion; acceptance is a separate host action.
Evidence is limited to repository identity, remote origin and qualified name. A shared display name never produces a suggestion.
Same-ecosystem duplicates are excluded unless includeSameEcosystem is set, because a source's own duplicates are that source's problem.
Live account evidence blocked: no authorized AWS credentials and no gateway in this environment

MCP 2026-07-28 only; the gateway's legacy revisions (2025-11-25, 2025-06-18, 2025-03-26) use the initialize handshake and belong to the MCP runtime client, reported as a blocking version issue rather than downgraded
The control-plane endpoint host is never composed: the adapter uses the binding's approved destination, because the AWS General Reference endpoint table could not be retrieved (JS-rendered)
The SigV4 signing service name defaults to bedrock-agentcore and is overridable in binding settings; it is unverified against a published endpoint table
Schemas stored in Amazon S3 are not fetched (S3 is not an approved destination); such targets are reported as unverifiable rather than assumed compatible

Smithy model, MCP server, API Gateway and built-in connector targets are synchronized by the gateway, so tool identities must come from tools/list; they are reported as requires-configuration, not invented
Swagger 2.0 is rejected outright, matching the documented support for OpenAPI 3.0 and 3.1 only
Live account evidence blocked: no authorized Google Cloud project, connection or token in this environment

Entity writes (create, patch, delete, updateEntitiesWithConditions, deleteEntitiesWithConditions), executeSqlQuery, executeHttpRequest, the v2 tools surface and eventing are deliberately not bound; only entity list/get, action execute and the metadata reads are

Long-running results: the connection-level asyncOperationsEnabled flag is surfaced and an action result on such a connection is returned with code google-connectors.async-result-unreconciled, never as settled work. The completion/poll mechanism for an async action is connector-specific and could not be verified from the discovery documents or the public docs: marked unverified
Connections are never created, updated, suspended or deleted; endUserAuthentication resources are not written

Region and location confusion is enforced against the documented public host patterns (bedrock-agentcore-control.<region>.amazonaws.com, connectors.<region>.rep.googleapis.com); a private or loopback host takes its region from the binding, which the fixtures exercise
Private-endpoint policy is enforced at the binding boundary (approved-private destination required); Ceremony never creates the VPC, Lattice or Service Directory resources involved

configure() requires a host ConfigurationWriter that consumes a secretRef from the existing private collection path; no writer is wired here, so the route reports configure.unavailable until the integrator supplies one
The default ConnectorPolicy denies every agent action unless a delegation store is supplied; hosts with a different delegation model must supply their own policy

Only profiles the v1 runtime can actually drive become methods: oauth-authorization-code -> oauth-code, api-key -> api-key, http-basic -> basic, oauth-device -> device. A definition with no drivable profile throws rather than fabricating a method (verified by test).
recoverable is false: the adapter keeps no protocol state of its own (the command service owns it), so the durable controller path is not opted into.
The events mount point delegates to an injected receiveEvent hook (EVENT swarm); with no hook the path answers 404 rather than accepting an unauthenticated delivery.
The fixture provider is a loopback double on an ephemeral port: it proves wire correctness and command discipline, never live or vendor-certified behaviour.
Toolkit, auth config, connected account and tool are four separate discovery scopes; a toolkit never implies an account and a service slug never replaces a native identifier.
Composio states no version for an auth config or a connected account. Those rows carry the explicit sentinel "unversioned" plus a composio.version.absent issue rather than an inferred version.
The Composio user_id is derived (HMAC or SHA-256 over tenant + owner kind + owner id, prefixed cer_) and is never read from a request, a scope selector or a model argument.
Live account evidence blocked: no authorized Composio project credentials in this execution.

Only hosted OAuth auth configs are driven. An API_KEY auth config returns {kind: "unsupported", code: "composio.auth-scheme.not-hosted"} because completing it would require submitting the end user's credential to Composio.

POST /api/v3/connected_accounts/link (auth link sessions) is documented but its request and response schemas were not retrievable at the recorded time, so no request is constructed for it. It is listed in composioUnimplementedEndpoints.
POST /api/v3/connected_accounts/{nanoid}/refresh is documented as deprecated; reconnect issues a fresh authorization instead.
connection.state.val is sent as an empty object: it carries per-scheme dynamic fields and this adapter collects no provider credential.
The hosted authorization URL is only carried in HandoffIssue.private and is checked against the binding's `connect` destination origin before it is stored.
A binding that pins connected accounts in permittedTargets cannot mint a new one (composio.account.pin-blocks-new): a new nanoid cannot appear in a list approved earlier.

Router meta tools are disabled unless the binding lists each one in settings.metaTools; the default is empty and COMPOSIO_MANAGE_CONNECTIONS, COMPOSIO_MULTI_EXECUTE_TOOL, COMPOSIO_REMOTE_BASH_TOOL and COMPOSIO_REMOTE_WORKBENCH are additionally classified as unrestricted.
A session whose tool_router_tools advertise anything outside the binding's tool and meta-tool allowlists is refused outright (composio.session.meta-tool-unapproved), so the session is never used.
The POST /tool_router/session/{id}/execute_meta request body is reused from the documented sibling execute body and is UNVERIFIED; the endpoint path and method are documented.
The value shapes of the documented session-create fields toolkits, auth_configs and connected_accounts are inferred (array of slugs; slug->id maps); the field names are documented.
POST /api/v3/tool_router/session/{id}/proxy_execute is deliberately not bound: a credentialed generic proxy is a confused deputy.

REVOKED and DELETED are accepted as connected-account statuses on SDK evidence only; they are not enumerated in the retrieved v3 reference and are marked unverified. An unrecognised status maps to indeterminate, never to a usable state.
DELETED maps to reconnect-required: the broker no longer holds the account, but no observation says the provider grant was revoked.
Composio documents no operation that revokes the end user's grant at the third-party provider, so revoke() reports upstream: "unsupported" and performs no call.
Broker disconnect deletes the connected account permanently and is refused unless the deployment passes allowBrokerDeletion: true; the default answer is broker: "unsupported" with no request sent.
Version drift is checked per (binding revision, tool slug, version) with a five-minute cache; a binding that pins "latest" opts out of the check, which is recorded rather than hidden.
Contracts validate description shape only; no adapter, transport or persistence behaviour is proven here
Round trips are exercised against real v1 projects built in-process; no HTTP import/export route is involved at this layer
The schema proves a claim's shape and internal consistency; whether an issuer actually observed what it reports is an adapter and command-layer obligation
Canaries are asserted absent from projection output; server-side logging, error bodies and storage are other swarms' surfaces
The refinement constrains how an issue may be reported; it cannot verify that an importer classified a construct correctly
JSON Schema checks structure only; every cross-field refinement is runtime-only and is asserted as such in CON-06-04

The public Airbyte API documents no source check_connection operation; verify() infers reachability from a live (ignoreCache=true) stream-properties discovery and records that limitation on the claim. The deprecated Configuration API (/api/v1/sources/check_connection, discover_schema) is deliberately not called: Airbyte documents it as internal and unsupported.
Documented job types are sync and reset only; the job type comes from the approved operation and can never be supplied by input.
Live account evidence blocked: no authorized Airbyte deployment credentials in this environment.
Records never flow through Ceremony; the adapter delegates jobs and reads status, it does not move data.
Pinned to ndc-spec ^0.2.0, implemented against 0.2.5 (latest in the published changelog on 2026-09-18). A connector declaring 0.1.x is blocked with a version diagnostic rather than downgraded.

POST /query/explain, POST /mutation/explain, GET /metrics, query variables and grouping (Grouping/dimensions) are not exercised by the bounded adapter; they are declared capabilities the policy simply never requests.
Relational query/mutation capabilities introduced in 0.2.1-0.2.3 are preserved as declarations but not executed.
Live evidence blocked: no authorized NDC connector deployment.

Merge documents passthrough as a Professional/Enterprise plan feature and per-integration (passthrough_available); the adapter honours the binding's fixed route and reports the upstream refusal rather than working around it.

Merge documents no operation that revokes the end user's upstream grant, so disconnect(upstream) reports 'unsupported'; POST /{category}/v1/delete-account is wired as the separate 'broker' scope only.
Write operations (POST/PATCH of category models) are not implemented; only bounded reads plus separately governed passthrough. /meta/post is read for field availability, not to perform writes.
Live account evidence blocked: no authorized Merge account, no real Link session.
No indexer and no crawler: Ceremony describes and evaluates ACLs, it does not build a retrieval index.
MembershipPort is an interface with in-memory conformance doubles; binding it to a real directory or identity connector is host work.
Cloud Search's own query-time serving is not reimplemented; this is an ACL-preserving descriptor and a conservative evaluator informed by the documented model.
All doubles are loopback HTTP fixtures on ephemeral ports written from published documentation; none is vendor certification and none contacts a real service.
The doubles implement the documented routes only; an undocumented path answers 404 exactly as an unknown route would.

The profile describes the code as it stands on this branch; it is not a conformance claim against any specification, and the Overlay JSONPath subset in particular is explicitly not RFC 9535 conformance
Examples are validated against the runtime Zod contracts only; a published example proves the contract accepts it, not that any adapter produces it
Every dialect claim is protocol-fixture or unit evidence: no live or vendor-certified behaviour is described anywhere

Licences were established for seven specification families by reading the published document or its LICENSE file on 2026-09-18; for every other record the licence field says `not-read-here` and claims no reuse beyond citation
Only one record carries a captured document digest (server-json-2025-12-11); no other swarm captured one, and the lock says so per record rather than inventing digests

The lock is pinned as of the ledgers named in `coversLedgers`, which at the time of writing is every ledger on disk with a resolvable source list and a coverage report of zero gaps. A ledger delivered afterwards may cite an unpinned identifier; the generator reports that as a coverage gap and the test asserts the gap is visible rather than silently accepted
An adapter factory that cannot be constructed with no host configuration has no machine-readable row; the generator names the module and the reason instead of guessing at its dimensions
Rows are measured with `capabilities(new Set())`, which is what a deployment holding no configuration sees; a configured deployment's directory can legitimately differ
Evidence per adapter is the strongest level any ledger recorded for that adapter's module directory, which is coarser than per-work-item evidence
Operational guidance, not an executable artifact: it has no test of its own. Every factual claim in it traces to a ledger or to the generated support matrix
It cannot be verified against a live deployment, because no authorized vendor credentials exist in this environment

Only claims that were verified false against the code were changed. Statements that are still accurate were left alone, including that generation and discovery are not exposed over MCP and that the reference application does not mount the in-chat collector

No provider-certification statement was strengthened: the MCP HTTP authorization and token-exchange rows now read 'implemented outbound (protocol fixture, not live)', which is exactly the evidence the OAUTH and MCP ledgers record and is not a live claim
docs/architecture.md was read and left unchanged: nothing in it was found to be factually stale

Test results come only from the JUnit run that scripts/connector-evidence.ts last recorded in report.json. At generation time that run recorded zero suites, so every test row reads 'not in the recorded run' and the report says so in bold rather than implying a pass
Requirement status is read from the ledgers at generation time, so it is current; it is a swarm's own claim about its work, joined to test results that are measured independently
The report does not run tests itself, by design: other swarms were running concurrently and a shared full-suite run would have collided with them
Channels, messages and operations become event descriptors only; an AsyncAPI operation is never compiled into an HTTP capability, so capabilities is always empty for this ecosystem.

transport "http-webhook" is claimed only for an inbound operation whose every declared protocol is http/https; ws, wss, kafka, amqp, mqtt, googlepubsub and every other binding keep transport "unsupported" with nativeTransport preserved. No broker runtime is implemented.
Only local JSON-pointer $ref resolution; an external or cross-document reference is reported as structure.unresolved-reference and never fetched.
Message payload schemas are preserved by reference (messageSchemaRef) rather than expanded, so a recursive schema is bounded by construction.
Channel parameters, reply objects and correlationId are preserved only inside the document-level native extension, not as first-class descriptor fields.
Perspective (consumer vs provider) is an explicit option; it is never inferred from operation or channel names.

toCloudEvent maps only id, source, type, time, datacontenttype and data. receivedAt is custody time, not occurrence time, and is never emitted as `time`; verification, connectionRef and forwarderHops have no CloudEvents attribute and are not smuggled in as extensions.

fromCloudEvent returns an explicitly UnverifiedEvent (no verification, no authority): a CloudEvent carries no proof, so reading one can never produce a verified envelope. Mapping `source` to a configured authority is a host decision.
CloudEvents binary mode (data_base64) is refused with ConnectorError("unsupported"); only the JSON event format is supported.
Only specversion 1.0 is accepted.

Only the symmetric v1 scheme (HMAC-SHA256) is implemented. The asymmetric v1a (ed25519) scheme is recognized and reported as "unsupported-scheme" rather than silently ignored; whsk_/whpk_ keys are not handled.
Timestamp tolerance defaults to 300s and is bounded to 1..86400s in both directions; a host cannot configure the window away.

verifyHmacHeader covers the common HMAC-over-body (optionally over `${timestamp}.${body}`) vendor pattern. A provider whose scheme differs implements VendorVerifierPort directly; nothing guesses a header name or algorithm.

No exactly-once claim. A handler that succeeded but whose fence was superseded leaves the entry pending, so a consumer may see the same authority-scoped deliveryId again and must deduplicate on it. This is asserted, not hidden, in the PostgreSQL concurrency test.

A contended lease (PersistenceConflict, or a PostgreSQL deadlock on the shared claims table) is counted as `skipped` and retried on the next pass; nothing has been delivered at that point, so no effect can be lost or duplicated by skipping.
Ordering is decided from the sender's sourceTime against a per-(authority, connection) watermark. An envelope with no sourceTime is "unknown" ordering and is applied normally.
The dispatcher reconciles only deliveries that carry a lifecycle signal; a non-lifecycle event arriving out of order is applied, because its payload is not a status claim.

The receiver requires a registered VendorVerifierPort for any non-Standard-Webhooks subscription; an unregistered verifier fails closed with 401 and audit reason "verifier-unavailable". There is no fallback scheme.
The delivery identity must come from the verifier, a policy.identify hook or a top-level `type`/id in the payload; an event that cannot be identified is refused 400 rather than given an invented id.

The receiver only admits. Applying a lifecycle event to a connection is the COMMAND swarm's dispatch hook (CompletionInput { kind: "event" }); lifecycle mapping here is a hint carried on the delivery.
Body ceiling is 256KiB by default, enforced while streaming (a content-length hint alone is not trusted).
Only JSON content types are accepted (configurable); form-encoded provider webhooks are not supported.

Vercel's outgoing trigger signature header name and algorithm are not published in the Connect triggers documentation (it states only that Vercel signs the forwarded request and publishes a per-connector signing key). verifyForwardedDelivery therefore takes the forwarder's VendorVerifierPort as an injected dependency; the VERCEL swarm supplies the concrete header/algorithm from its own source. The fixture verifier used in tests is explicitly a stand-in, not a claim about Vercel's wire format.

The original provider's hop is verified only when this deployment holds that provider's secret (material keys prefixed `upstream:`); otherwise no provider hop is recorded at all rather than an assumed one.

Readers take an already-parsed document; bytes-to-object parsing (JSON/YAML bounds, duplicate keys, dangerous tags) belongs to the IMPORT swarm. The adapter's default parser accepts JSON only and re-serializes to strip prototype keys.
External $ref resolution happens only through the caller's resolveExternal hook; without one, constructs behind an external reference are reported unresolved and blocked, never guessed.
Reference fragments are RFC 6901 JSON pointers only; plain-name anchors, $anchor, $dynamicRef and $recursiveRef are refused rather than approximated.
3.2 additionalOperations and QUERY operations are read and preserved, but no non-standard method can be bound (see HTTP-03).

Examples, defaults and credential-named vendor keys are dropped from preserved extensions at the import boundary; a vendor extension with a neutral key that embeds a secret in an unnamed field would still be preserved for reviewers.

An openIdConnect issuer is derived only when openIdConnectUrl ends in the standard /.well-known/openid-configuration suffix; any other spelling becomes an unsupported profile with a blocking issue rather than a guessed issuer.
mutualTLS is preserved as a mutual-tls profile but blocks authorization: this runtime holds no client certificates.
The OAuth implicit and password flows are preserved as unsupported profiles with blocking issues (RFC 9700); no usable credential path is invented for them.
The device authorization flow exists only in 3.2; the same flow object under 3.0/3.1 becomes an unsupported profile with a blocking security.unknown-flow issue.

Executable subset: application/json (and +json) request and response bodies; path and header parameters style simple; query parameters style form with explode honoured and allowReserved respected; primitives and arrays of primitives only.

Blocked with serialization.* issues: multipart, form-urlencoded, XML, streaming and any other media type; cookie parameters; 3.2 querystring parameters; parameters described by content; deepObject, spaceDelimited, pipeDelimited, matrix and label styles.

Schema subset validated: type (including 3.1/3.2 type arrays and 3.0 nullable), enum, const, required, properties, items, additionalProperties, min/max length, items, properties, numeric bounds, multipleOf, uniqueItems and basic formats. allOf/anyOf/oneOf/not/if-then-else, pattern, patternProperties, prefixItems, contains, unevaluated*, discriminator and dynamic references block the operation that uses them.

A pure $ref alias cycle (A -> B -> A with no concrete schema) is reported as an unresolved reference and blocks that operation; a structurally recursive schema (a node containing itself) compiles into a named definitions table and validates to an explicit depth.
Only the seven methods the binding contract carries can be bound; 3.2 QUERY and additionalOperations entries stay discoverable but block with structure.unsupported-method.
A path parameter value containing '/' is refused (openapi.path-parameter-encoded-slash): %2F containment inside the approved prefix cannot be proven across intermediaries.

Credentials come from ctx.environment.credentials.use only. The adapter reads apiKey/username/password/accessToken (optionally suffixed ':<profileId>' when several profiles are presented together); the integrator's credential layer must write those names.

Bound authentication profiles are read from binding.settings['openapi-http-profiles']; an alternative naming a profile the binding does not carry fails with configuration-required rather than falling back to another alternative.
Verification is available only when the host names an approved read operation as verifier, and it claims credential-accepted against the destination origin — never account identity.
No upstream disconnect or revoke exists in an OpenAPI description; both report local scope only and 'unsupported' upstream.
Events are unsupported in this adapter: webhooks and callbacks are imported as descriptions, and verified delivery belongs to the events profile.

The JSONPath subset is: root ($), child by name (.name and ['name'] / ["name"]), wildcard (.* and [*]), recursive descent (..name and ..*) and non-negative array index ([0]). RFC 9535 filters, scripts, unions, slices, negative indexes and function extensions are refused with a blocking structure.unsupported-selector issue rather than approximated. The Overlay specification requires full RFC 9535 for interoperability, so this is an explicit, documented subset, not a conformance claim.
Selection, merge depth, action count and update size are bounded; exceeding a bound refuses the whole overlay rather than applying part of it.
A document that cannot be serialized within bounds (for example one whose shared references expand exponentially) is refused with structure.document-too-large instead of throwing.
Export emits OpenAPI 3.1 only; a document imported as 2.0, 3.0 or 3.2 is republished in 3.1 spelling and the version change is part of the loss report.

Response schemas are emitted as permissive (`true`) rather than reproduced: the compiled subset keeps request schemas for validation but does not validate responses, and publishing a response schema the runtime does not enforce would overstate the contract.
Without a binding the export carries no operations at all, because no executable surface has been approved.
Native extensions are withheld unless the operator explicitly asks for them.

The WorkOS user and organization identifiers come from a host-supplied WorkOsPrincipalPort keyed by tenant+ownerKind+ownerId; an organization connection additionally requires organizationConnection === "permitted". A deployment without that port cannot use this adapter, by design.
A connected account with no account_identifier yields an ownership-claimed claim, not account-identity: the broker showed a connection, not which upstream account it is.
Live account evidence blocked: no authorized WorkOS environment credentials.

Refresh remains WorkOS's responsibility: the documentation states the token endpoint always returns a valid, refreshed token, so this adapter re-vends instead of refreshing upstream. When WorkOS omits expires_at the credential is stored under a bounded local lease (default 900 s).

Relay operations are bound HTTP operations: a path parameter that contains a slash cannot be expressed as one segment because `destinationUrl` refuses encoded slashes; model such targets as separate path segments (e.g. {owner}/{repository}).
The relay upstream response is bounded (default 1 MiB) and returned as {status, body}; streaming passthrough is not implemented.
Live Relay evidence blocked: Relay is early access and no authorized environment was available.

The subject token and the My Account API token come from a host-supplied HostIdentityTokenPort; a deployment without myAccountToken cannot list or link accounts and the adapter reports configuration-required rather than working around it.

The upstream provider token is usually opaque, so `tokenClaimsVerified` is false for it; when the returned token is a JWS with a key id it is verified against the tenant JWKS and refused if it does not verify.
Account selection requires an explicit host-approved target in binding.permittedTargets; several linked accounts with no selection yields human-required, never a heuristic choice.
Live tenant evidence blocked: no authorized Auth0 tenant.
A reconnect link is produced through the Connected Accounts connect endpoint; when the deployment holds no My Account token the mapping still reports reconnect-required, without a link.
unsupported_grant_type is reported as ConnectorError("unsupported", "auth0.grant.unsupported"): an unavailable grant is a configuration fact, and no second grant is attempted.
Fixtures are recorded documented payloads, not captured live traffic; each file records its source URL and retrieval date.

YAML is read only as YAML 1.2 with the core schema. An explicit %YAML 1.1 directive is refused rather than reinterpreted, because 1.1 changes the meaning of unquoted yes/no/on/off and of sexagesimal scalars.

Explicit !!binary, !!timestamp, !!omap, !!set and !!pairs tags are refused even though the library could resolve them: a connector description has no use for them, and silently keeping the text of an unresolved tag is the reinterpretation import must not do.
Merge keys (<<) are refused rather than applied; a description that relies on them must be flattened upstream.
A document is one YAML document; a multi-document stream is refused instead of silently using the first.

An end-to-end connection to an administrator-approved private origin cannot be demonstrated offline: a loopback fixture binds to 127.0.0.0/8, which classifies as loopback, not private. The approved-private path is covered by policy assertions plus a DNS-level assertion that an approved origin reaches the transport while an unapproved sibling is refused at the lookup.
Request bodies must be fully buffered (bounded by maxRequestBytes); stream and multipart bodies are refused, because neither can be bounded up front nor replayed across a validated redirect.
TLS certificate pinning is not part of this fetcher; it inherits the platform trust store through undici.
Only JSON pointer fragments resolve. A plain-name fragment ($anchor, #Pet) and a JSON Schema $id-relative base are reported as unsupported rather than guessed at.
$id/$anchor rebasing within a document is not implemented; documents are addressed by the identity they were registered under.

The security classification is pointer-pattern based and covers OpenAPI 2/3, AsyncAPI, Arazzo sourceDescriptions and MCP server.json packages/remotes. A format whose security semantics live elsewhere needs its rule added; unmatched changes are reported as structural, never dropped.
Array comparison is positional, so a reordered servers list reports changes at the moved indexes rather than as a move.
AC-IMP-06 is covered here only for the source-diff half; overlay application belongs to the FORMATS swarm.
These are pure helpers over ports. HTTP routing, CSRF/origin checks and multipart decoding are the COMMAND swarm's; importUpload takes bytes that the host has already bounded.
detectDocument recognizes the family and version only. Normalization into a NormalizedDefinition is the FORMATS swarm's, so every result currently returns empty definitions and executableCandidates.

The reference server's connector actor is derived from its anonymous session cookie; a deployment authenticates before the route table is reached, which is why the handler takes an actor rather than deriving one.

No adapter is configured in the reference server, so every provider-backed row reports unconfigured. That is the honest state for a server that has signed up for nothing, not a missing implementation.

The consumer is built by unpacking the tarball rather than by npm install: installing pulls runtime dependencies from a registry and one postinstall downloads a native binary, which this environment cannot reach. So the export map and the published file set are proven; the dependency set a fresh install would produce is not.

PR #39 is another author's open pull request and was not merged, rebased or pushed to. The reconciliation is an audit recorded in docs/connector-directory.md and a replacement surface on this branch; whether to close #39 is its author's decision.

Mutation testing over the connector guards is not wired: stryker.security.config.mjs has no connector guard targets yet, so the killers run in the ordinary security suite but no connector guard is mutated.
Live and deployed oracles are all blocked. No authorized credential and no operator consent exists here, and nothing is labelled live.
The profile is selected by the binding's settings, never by the installed SDK version; the SDK is used only to build the legacy fixture server.
Auto-detection is off unless a binding sets compatibility to auto-detect; a pinned client refuses a server of the other era rather than accommodating it.
stdio transports are unsupported by design: a hosted connector launches no local process.
Completion (completion/complete) and logging are not implemented; they are not needed to bind an approved operation.
Resource subscriptions are read through a bounded listen stream; there is no durable event pipeline (that belongs to the events module).
Only form-mode elicitation is answered with values; URL mode produces a browser handoff for the initiating human and the client never fetches the URL.
A sampling request is refused rather than suspended, in either era.
Rounds are bounded (three by default); a server that keeps asking is failed, not looped.
Reconciliation of an indeterminate effect is the command layer's: this adapter records the uncertainty and refuses to repeat the call.
Retries exist only for reads and only for a request that was not delivered or whose response was lost; there is no retry budget for writes at all.
Protocol retries, HTTP retries and business reconciliation are separate: a repeated effect digest is answered from the journal without touching the network.
The four tools are a transport over a service the command swarm owns; they enforce projection and output policy, not authorization, which the service re-checks.
connector_invoke returns output only when the binding classified it public; personal and secret results are withheld from this transport and remain readable in the application.
Live authorized evidence is blocked: no credentials for a deployed MCP server are available in this environment.
verify establishes that the credential was accepted by the origin and says explicitly that server identity is not attested beyond TLS.
authorize delegates to the OAuth swarm's beginOAuth hook; with a bearer already in custody it returns verify without contacting an authorization server.
disconnect is local only and revoke is unsupported: MCP defines no such operation.
Swagger 2.0 only, which is the only version the Power Platform importer accepts; an OpenAPI 3.x document is refused with a blocking version diagnostic rather than half-imported
Native capability effect and data classification are reported as unknown: Swagger 2.0 declares neither, and an HTTP method is not evidence of an effect
Entra ID (identityProvider "aad") connection parameters yield an authorization-code profile with no endpoints; loginUri/tenantId are preserved but no authorize or token URL is synthesized from them
Request and response schemas are referenced by pointer, not copied into the definition; the protected source artifact remains authoritative for them

A dynamic operation that is not a GET or HEAD is compiled with effect unknown and replay none, with a policy.dynamic-operation-effect-unknown warning, instead of being asserted read-only from the extension alone
Option caching is in-process by default (createMemoryDynamicCache); a deployment supplies a DynamicOptionCachePort with the same key discipline
Dynamic values are executed only for a contract the binding carries; a contract supplied by a caller is refused
A parameterized test-connection path is refused rather than guessed: verify throws unsupported with detail microsoft.verify.parameterized
The claim's target id is the binding's approved connectorId (or the connection's service), never an upstream account identifier

Webhook triggers are described, not subscribed: the adapter implements no events port, and the descriptor's verification is "unknown" until a host approves a receiver and a delivery verification method

Polling triggers have no equivalent trigger state in Ceremony (the Power Platform holds the cursor in a Location header across 202 responses), so they are transport "unsupported" with nativeTransport "polling" and a blocking diagnostic

An on-premises gateway requirement is reported under category "network" rather than "policy": it is a network-path requirement, not code. Custom code uses "executable-code" and policy templates use "policy" as the brief specifies
The export reproduces no request or response schema: the description carries pointers, not schemas, and every affected operation gets an explicit loss
apiProperties.json and script.csx are not produced; connection parameters, client secrets and connection values never leave in an export
Extensions that lived inside a body or response schema have no reproduced schema to attach to and are reported as unplaced rather than moved somewhere else

invoke executes approved dynamic field lookups only; any other bound operation is refused so the adapter cannot become a credentialed fetch(url, headers, body) escape hatch. Ordinary operations belong to the HTTP adapter under their own binding

No events, authorize, complete, reconnect, disconnect, revoke or delegate: the connector's credential lifecycle belongs to the OAuth and state work, and the adapter reports those dimensions honestly rather than stubbing them
support defaults to "provider-backed" with no adapter-level configuration; a deployment may override it when registering a fixture instance
GET /integrations documents no pagination parameters; the adapter pages the returned array client-side with an opaque cursor that carries its own page size.
Integration client credentials are never requested (include=credentials is never sent), so discovery cannot report OAuth client ids or scopes configured in Nango.

Per-integration auth requirements are reported as the two external-broker profiles plus the function metadata Nango exposes; Nango does not publish a per-integration auth-mode field on these endpoints.

A connect session alone proves only that Nango holds a connection for the bound integration. Exact-account intents require an approved read-only verification operation in the binding; without one an exact-account intent is denied rather than relabelled verified (AC-AUTH-08).
Reconnect completion needs either an HMAC-verified auth/override webhook or a prior auth error that clears in GET /connections; Nango publishes no reconnect-specific server state to poll.
The connect_link is accepted only when its origin equals the approved connect destination.

Reading this endpoint can refresh the upstream token as a documented side effect; the adapter cannot make it side-effect free, so it records refreshMayHaveOccurred: true on every inspection and serialises the call through the custody port's single-flight refresh.
Bounded metadata only: metadata deeper or larger than the configured bounds is dropped and reported as metadataOmitted rather than stored.
Base-Url-Override, Retries, Retry-On and Decompress are never sent from caller input; Retries is set only from the approved contract and only for read-only operations.
X-Async is not used: the async action result schema is not published, so an unexpected async envelope is treated as indeterminate rather than parsed.
A 5xx from Nango on a non-read operation whose replay policy is 'none' is reported indeterminate, because Nango may already have forwarded the request upstream.
Nango documents no endpoint to cancel a running sync execution; 'cancel' maps to POST /sync/pause (pausing the schedule) and the result says so explicitly via nango.sync.cancel-maps-to-pause.
opts.reset and opts.emptyCache are refused: they clear Nango's checkpoints and record cache, which is a data-destroying operation this adapter does not expose.
Sync execution, scheduling and checkpointing remain Nango's; nothing here reimplements them.

The legacy X-Nango-Signature header is ignored even when correct, per the documentation's own guidance; NANGO_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_KEY is required for the events dimension and the Environment API key is never used as a fallback.

No shared event inbox was available from the EVENT swarm at implementation time, so dedupe uses a bounded in-process inbox (authority-scoped, 4096 entries, 1 hour window). The adapter accepts an injected inbox through NangoAdapterOptions.eventInbox and the integrator should supply the durable one.
Nango documents no upstream grant revocation endpoint, so revoke reports 'unsupported' rather than deleting the broker connection and calling it revocation.
Exact issuer comparison only: no trailing-slash or case tolerance, by design.
Signed metadata (`signed_metadata`) is not verified; documents are trusted only through transport plus the exact issuer match.
Metadata cache is in-process per deployment; the STATE swarm owns any shared-cache variant.
S256 PKCE only; an issuer advertising only `plain` is reported unsupported rather than downgraded.
DPoP is not applied by this module; src/server/authored-oauth.ts holds the existing DPoP seam and the two are not yet joined.
Device poll state is returned in CompletionResult.adapterState; the command layer must persist it for the interval and slow_down backoff to hold across calls.

CIMD revision implemented: draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-03 (observed 2026-09-17). The document body is produced by the existing clientMetadataDocument() in src/server/authored-oauth.ts and is not duplicated here.
The CIMD document must be served by the host at the returned clientId; this module returns the artifact and its storage key but does not mount the route (integrator-owned).
DCR uses client_secret_basic/post or none; private_key_jwt registration is not requested dynamically.
Registration-access-token lifecycle (RFC 7592 update/delete) is stored but not exercised.
validatePopupCompletion is the server-side rule only; the UX swarm owns the browser listener that feeds it an event's origin and the opener's window id.
Accepting a popup message authorizes exactly one thing: a server verification call. It is never itself completion.
VerificationClaim.permissions.observed is always [] here: observation belongs to a verifier that calls a real operation, not to the grant.
Introspection-sourced `reported` scopes are produced only on the token-exchange path; the code path uses the token response `scope`.
reviewPermissionEscalation compares against the previously *requested* set, so a provider grant wider than the review never silently becomes the new baseline.
ID-JAG (urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id-jag) is unsupported by default and requires tokenExchange.idJag in host policy; the code is oauth.exchange.id-jag-not-negotiated.
An opaque issued token is verified only when the issuer publishes an introspection endpoint; otherwise the exchange is refused as unverifiable rather than trusted.
JWT verification requires an asymmetric alg and the issuer's jwks_uri; symmetric-signed tokens are refused.
Live account evidence blocked: no authorized Pipedream project credentials in this environment.

The external user id is a server-side HMAC/SHA-256 digest of tenant + owner kind + owner id, prefixed cer_. It is never accepted from input, and an optional host key (options.externalUserKey) makes it unguessable outside the deployment.
An unavailable account listing is reported as connectedAccounts: "unknown" plus a compatibility issue, never as zero.

Pipedream's connect token cannot be restricted to one app at the API level; the documented restriction point is the Connect Link / SDK `app` parameter, which the adapter sets from the binding. The host-side guarantee is that a completion only ever binds an account whose app equals the binding's app; any other account is refused.
Connection webhooks are unsigned, so they are accepted only as untrusted hints (CompletionInput 'input') that trigger a trusted server query; they are never accepted as verified events.
Account-identity evidence is the broker's record for the derived external user; Ceremony does not query the third-party provider, and the claim's limitations say so.
A host-supplied idempotencyKey is refused: Pipedream documents no idempotency key for /actions/run or /triggers/deploy, so accepting one would claim evidence that does not exist.
A lost or 5xx/504 response to a write is reported indeterminate and must be reconciled; the adapter never retries it automatically.
Component descriptions are imported as inert NativeCapability descriptors; no component source is fetched or evaluated. File Stash components are execution-blocked with a precise diagnostic.
Dynamic props (configure/reload) are not bound: props whose reloadProps is true must be fixed in the binding, reported as a requires-configuration issue on import.

Deduplication is host-side: a stable digest of tenant + connection + external user + project + environment + component + version + configured props keys the effect journal, and before deploying the adapter looks for an equivalent trigger already held for that external user. Equivalence compares the component key and the canonical JSON of configured props with the app prop removed; a broker that normalizes prop values differently would not match, and the adapter would then deploy (the journal still prevents a repeat of the same command).
A deploy whose outcome cannot be reconciled stays indeterminate and is never retried automatically; an operator must resolve the journal entry.

The signing key returned by a deploy is stored in credential custody, and the reference is returned in the invoke output as output.delivery.signingKeyRef. EventPort.verify reads references from connection.state.pipedreamTriggerKeys, so the command layer must copy that reference onto the connection (see integrationPatches).
EventPort.subscribe/unsubscribe are not implemented: deploying a trigger needs configured props, so it is an approved operation rather than a generic subscription.
revoke() reports upstream: unsupported. Pipedream documents no endpoint that revokes the end user's grant at the third-party provider; the adapter does not silently delete the broker account instead.
Live account evidence blocked: no authorized Nango, Supabase, Vercel or registry credentials exist in this environment (see QA-06).

The MCP registry continuation marker could not be settled offline: the client reads metadata.nextCursor, the registry's REST examples have also circulated with next_cursor. Both spellings are served by the double and the consequence of the unrecognized one is recorded.
Supabase Management OAuth was verified by running the delivered suite rather than against a QA-owned double; the Supabase suites bind fixed port 4427 and were run sequentially and separately.
Runs against the fixture provider and the fixture adapter registered by the command harness; provider-specific oracles stay with the provider swarms' own suites.

Process restart is exercised at the durable boundary (the effect journal and the persisted intent), not by killing and relaunching a process: the harness builds its store and ports in one constructor and does not expose a second service over the same ports.
Rate limiting is exercised against a provider that answers 429 with Retry-After in the QA-01 suite; the command-level assertion here is limited to error sanitization and preserved state.
Reconnect with an explicit account-switch intent is covered by the COMMAND and NANGO suites; this suite asserts only that a switch cannot happen without one.
Property runs are bounded (300/200/120 runs) to keep the suite inside the shared machine's budget.
The packed-consumer half of AC-PKG-01 is asserted structurally in QA-05, not by running npm pack, which touches shared files.

The Playwright accessibility suites (tests/browser/connector-directory.spec.ts, connector-drawer.spec.ts) bind fixed ports 4173/4174 and were not executed: the charter forbids running browser suites while other swarms work. This suite asserts their presence, that they make keyboard and accessible-name assertions, and that they are reachable from npm run test:e2e.

npm run build, build:vercel and the packed-consumer pack were not executed: they touch shared build output and the bundle budget script, which are integrator-owned. AC-PKG-02 is covered here by a static import-graph walk instead of by inspecting a built artifact.
Workflow recovery lives in tests/workflow under vitest and is excluded from the node runner; it was not run.

Live account evidence blocked: no authorized credentials and no operator consent exist in this environment. Every one of the five manifest entries reports blocked, and the report names the exact missing prerequisite by environment-variable name.
The manifest is not yet wired into npm run verify:live; the exact integrator patch is in integrationPatches.
Live evidence blocked: tests never reach the network; the loopback double is authored from the published API documents.
ETag/conditional requests are not used; the documented aggregator pattern is hourly polling with updated_since.
Import refuses pre-2025-09-16 snake_case documents instead of translating them; a migration would be a separate reader.
URL template variables in remotes are preserved but never substituted at import time.
Collection is best effort inside its own transaction; a conflict leaves the abandoned generation for the next refresh to collect.
One in-flight refresh per source: a concurrent refresh fails with conflict/registry.refresh.concurrent rather than interleaving.
Public marks are supplied by the host (a digest set or a predicate); this swarm does not implement the UI or storage for marking an entry public.
The surfaces are functions over a snapshot; mounting them as HTTP routes is integrator-owned.
No live publication: the official registry source ships with publication disabled and no deployment token exists here.
Export describes remotes only; a deployment that wanted to publish a package would need evidence this swarm deliberately does not accept.

The directory row reports support 'provider-backed', not 'catalog-only': catalogEntrySchema refuses an implemented capability under 'catalog-only', and this adapter really does read a registry. The catalog-only boundary is reported per dimension instead.
authorize/invoke are unsupported by design; an MCP binding made by the MCP runtime swarm is the only path to execution.

Nine trust boundaries are modelled: imported data, hosted browser, private collector, Ceremony host to upstream, external broker, registry, event sender, optional runner, and tenant-to-tenant. Each carries an executable refusal against the real module; none is covered by a success stub.

The A2A delegation boundary and the WebMCP browser-local boundary are described in the ecosystem table but were not modelled here: their modules were still being written while this swarm tested (src/server/connectors/providers/a2a/* appeared untracked at 14:13 UTC).
Live-authorized evidence is blocked everywhere: no authorized provider credentials exist in this environment and tests have no internet.
XML entity expansion was not exercised: no XML reader is reachable from src/server/connectors/import, so there is nothing to attack there yet.

The parse-time budget (maxParseMs) is checked after the work rather than interrupting it; the structural bounds are what actually make pathological input impossible. Reported as designed, not as a defect.
Integration and environment confusion for brokers is covered for Nango only (SEC-04); Composio, Pipedream, WorkOS and Smithery were still being written when this swarm tested and were not attacked.

RFC 8414 signed_metadata and signed RFC 9728 resource metadata are read but not signature-verified (OAUTH swarm's own unmet item OA-01-signed-metadata); this swarm confirms the gap rather than closing it.

Shared-grant revocation across several local connections (AC-STATE-04) is asserted by the STATE and COMMAND swarms' own suites; this swarm did not add an independent reproduction because the shared-grant record shape lives in src/server/connectors/state and was still moving during the run.
Broker token leakage is covered for Nango's credential-bearing connection read through the canary sweep and the NANGO swarm's AC-NG-03 test; no other broker adapter was stable enough to attack.

Logs and traces have no connector-specific sink in this checkout, so the canary sweep covers the projections, the error explanation, the audit row, the published registry document and the service worker rather than a log transport. The invariant enforced instead is that every structured value that could reach a log is built by an allowlist projection.
Browser storage is asserted negatively at the source level (no localStorage, sessionStorage or indexedDB use anywhere under src/), not by driving a browser; the UX swarm owns the browser assertions.
stryker.security.config.mjs and .github/workflows/verify.yml are integrator-owned; the exact patch is in integrationPatches and was not applied by this swarm.

Until that patch lands, the killers run in the canonical suite through `npm run test:security` (scripts/test.mjs profile 'security' selects tests/connectors/security/*.test.ts by path) and through `npm test` / `test:coverage`, but the Stryker security matrix does not yet mutate the connector guards.

Excluding the whole entry is the existing policy for a private remote URL and is now applied to every published URL field. It is fail-closed and may over-exclude an entry whose websiteUrl or repository URL is plain http; the exclusion is reported with its reason, so an operator can see why. The REGISTRY swarm may prefer to drop the offending field instead for the non-executable fields.
Ownership beyond the subject/session rule is a host policy injected as `owns`; the state layer never derives organization or workload ownership from a record field.
Definition and binding records are tenant-scoped, not owner-scoped: they are descriptions, and the command layer applies review capability checks.

`use` refuses a result that contains material by value scan; a caller that deliberately transforms material (hashing, truncation below eight characters) is not detectable and remains the adapter author's responsibility.
External broker refresh remains the broker's responsibility; this port holds only the protected broker reference under the broker custody kind.
`EffectJournalPort.complete` accepts an outcome only from the worker that began the effect and still holds its lease; an orphaned effect is settled through `reconcile`, which takes the lease first.
Artifacts are stored inside the encrypted record value (base64), bounded to 8 MB by default; larger source bytes need an object store the host supplies.
The throttle is a bounded fixed window plus a circuit marker, in the shape of `reserveRequest`; it is not a token bucket and does not smooth bursts within a window.
AC-STATE-03 and AC-STATE-04 are covered here at the data-model level; the provider-facing halves (what a broker delete or an upstream revoke actually does on the wire) belong to the provider swarms.
The cache invalidation hook is best effort and runs after the durable change commits: a hook failure never undoes a committed invalidation.

The crash worker exercises death after begin and after complete; a kill inside the committing transaction is covered by the store's own rollback, already proven in tests/command-crash-boundaries.test.ts.

The Management API documents no pagination for GET /v1/organizations or GET /v1/projects; the adapter windows one bounded response and reports that as a discover issue rather than inventing page parameters
Access-token and refresh-token lifetimes are not documented; expiry is taken from the token response expires_in only
Organization-owned connections are out of scope: only ownerKind "user" is accepted, because an organization tag is not an organization grant
account-identity evidence depends on GET /v1/profile being permitted for the grant; when it is refused the connection keeps resource-access evidence and records the gap as a claim limitation
Protocol execution is delegated to the MCP swarm's client through McpClientPort; this profile owns the binding, the pinned URL and what may be asked, not the wire protocol
Token acquisition is delegated to McpAuthorizationPort; without a registered profile authorize reports unsupported instead of improvising a registration

No revoke: a dynamically registered client holds no secret for POST /v1/oauth/revoke, so the documented alternative (the user revokes the app in the Supabase dashboard) is recorded as a capability limitation
The per-tool feature-group table is taken from the published available-tools list; a server that adds a tool later is simply not in an approved binding
Reads only: bounded GET /rest/v1/<table> selects on approved tables, columns and filters; no insert, update, delete, RPC or embedded resource
Only the default exposed schema (public); another schema would need Accept-Profile and its own review
Row Level Security is the project's, not the adapter's; a table whose RLS review is unverified is flagged on every result and in the verification claim rather than being assumed safe
No revoke: the session belongs to the existing project sign-in ceremony, so signing out happens there
Live project evidence blocked: no authorized Supabase project in this environment
Foreign tables have no Row Level Security; the documented limitation is attached to every capability row, every descriptor table and every read result
readWrappersDescriptor never executes SQL: it reads catalog-style metadata, or parses migration DDL text statically under byte and statement ceilings
import foreign schema creates tables the migration text does not describe; the gap is reported as an issue and catalog metadata is required for column review
Reads run under the host's database role through ApprovedQueryPort, so there is no end-user grant and the authorize dimension is unsupported by design

patch.target: MCP runtime swarm: consuming imported remotes
patch.description: An imported definition is not bindable by itself. For each capability whose nativeId starts with 'mcp-remote:' (the executableCandidates of the import outcome), read nativeExtensions['io.modelcontextprotocol.registry/remote'] for { type: 'streamable-http' | 'sse', url, headers, variables }. Before a binding exists the reviewer must: resolve any {curly_brace} variables from host configuration (they are never substituted at import time), turn the resulting origin into an ApprovedDestination, map header inputs to the definition's configurationRequirements (X_API_KEY style names; non-conforming names are in io.ceremony.connectors/unsupported-configuration and need an explicit mapping), and create BoundOperations with transport kind mcp-tool/mcp-resource/mcp-prompt. Capabilities whose nativeId starts with 'mcp-package:' are never bindable: nativeExtensions['io.ceremony.connectors/execution'].approved is false and the definition carries a blocking policy.execution-requires-binding issue. Registry status is provenance, not code safety: a namespace-authenticated 'active' entry says who published, not that the server is safe.

patch.target: ports the MCP swarm must satisfy (INT/MCP)
patch.description: McpClientPort { listTools(session), callTool(session, { name, arguments }) } where McpServerSession carries { url, resource, protocol: "mcp-2026-07-28" | "mcp-2025-11-25", authorization: { kind: "bearer", use(work) } | { kind: "none" }, fetch, signal }. The bearer handle only lends the token inside a callback and refuses any credential that is not kind "hosted-mcp-access-token", so a management token cannot be forwarded to the MCP server. McpAuthorizationPort { begin(ctx, { serverUrl, resource, registration, protocol, credentialKind, intent }), complete(ctx, input, { serverUrl, resource }) } is the OAUTH swarm's registration profile (dynamic client registration is the documented default for the hosted server); it must store the token under credential kind "hosted-mcp-access-token".

patch.target: ports the COMMAND/state layer must satisfy (INT/COMMAND)
patch.description: ProjectSessionPort { resolve({ actor, connectionRef, projectRef, signal }) } returns the verified project-user session from the existing sign-in ceremony as { kind: "project-user-session", projectRef, userId, expiresAt, assurance?, use(work) }; the access token is lent inside the callback and never returned. Any other kind is refused as credential-kind confusion. ApprovedQueryPort { catalog({ signal }), select({ schema, table, columns, filters, order?, limit, offset, signal }) } executes the host's parameterized, allowlisted foreign-table read; it must refuse anything it cannot parameterize and must never accept a SQL string. The command layer also owns: issuing the proposed handoffs, persisting connections, and advancing the connection generation when an authorize/reconnect result carries a supersede report.

The four profiles are alternatives for one service and must be grouped, never merged: Management OAuth is a dashboard-user authority, the hosted MCP server is a separate OAuth resource, the Data API acts as a project user, and Wrappers runs under the host's database role with no end-user grant. Capability rows already carry the per-profile limitations (no pagination, unknown scopes, no foreign-table RLS, delegated protocol execution, no revoke route) for display.
